headline: High: shared filesystem and broad tool access make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A reads files, clipboard, screenshots, and app context; Agent B reads and writes workspace files and uses MCP. A can ingest B-authored content if copied or opened, and B can parse A outputs from shared files or screenshots. No explicit provenance or isolation is documented, so injection is plausible in default workflows.
conditions: IF A ingests text copied from B into chat or app context
IF B reads a file that A previously wrote or summarized
IF either agent treats shared workspace content as instructions
mitigations: Disable copy-paste bridges between agents for untrusted content
Use separate workspaces or folders per agent
Prefix all inter-agent artifacts with a non-executable format header
Manually review any file before the other agent consumes it

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches uploaded files, screenshots, voice, and connected IDE code, while B can write and read workspace files and has broad network egress. If sensitive material enters A, B can receive it through shared files or copied outputs and then transmit it outward. The pair lacks documented isolation, so leakage is a default-path concern.
conditions: IF sensitive files are opened in A and then saved into B's workspace
IF B is allowed to send workspace contents to external services
IF both agents operate on the same project directory
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of the shared workspace
Use separate OS accounts or profiles for each agent
Turn off network access for B when handling sensitive data
Redact secrets before passing artifacts between agents

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A cannot write files or modify git state, but B can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses in a shared workspace. That asymmetry still creates conflict because B can overwrite or commit around A's read-only assumptions, and A may act on stale state. The shared filesystem path is documented, so coordination bugs are credible.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repository or directory
IF B commits or rewrites files while A is reading them
IF A's screenshots or app context reflect stale filesystem state
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate branch or directory
Require B to pause before any git write
Use file locks or a single-writer rule
Have A refresh state before acting on file contents

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can summarize code, screenshots, and app context, and B can execute shell commands, modify git state, and use MCP. If B treats A's summaries as authoritative, A's mistakes can become code changes or external actions. The pair therefore supports a classic unverified handoff with potentially irreversible downstream effects.
conditions: IF B uses A's summary without re-reading the underlying files
IF A's output is pasted into B as the sole source of truth
IF B is permitted to commit or run commands based on A's claims
mitigations: Require B to verify every A-derived claim against source files
Use a checklist before any commit or shell action
Limit A to drafting only, not final instructions
Review diffs manually before execution

E_compliance.rationale: A is vendor-mediated and touches uploaded files, screenshots, voice, and connected IDE code; B is a local VS Code agent with workspace files and user-configured model provider/MCP calls. The profiles do not show a clear residency or certification mismatch, but B's broad egress and A's vendor-only backend create a small compliance gap if regulated data is introduced.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into either agent's workspace
IF B sends workspace contents to a non-approved provider or MCP server
IF retention or residency requirements apply to the shared artifacts
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared workspaces
Pin B to an approved provider and MCP allowlist
Document retention settings for both tools
Use separate projects for regulated and non-regulated work
